713534.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pʰógʷos, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰógʷos, from *bʰegʷ- (“to run, flee”). See φέβομαι (phébomai, “to flee”) for more.

713532.t: By surface analysis, φόβος (phóbos) + -έω (-éō). From Proto-Hellenic *pʰogʷéyō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰogʷéyeti, from *bʰegʷ-.

713578.t: Perhaps from either Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰren- (“soul, mind; innards, diaphragm”), whence Old Norse grunr (“suspicion”), or *bʰren- (“front edge”), whence e.g.

713541.t: The etymology surrounding all senses remains somewhat unclear. The fact that the dye came exclusively from Phoenicia assures some connection.

713518.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pʰlegō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to blaze, burn”). Cognates include Sanskrit भर्ग (bharga) and Latin flagrō.

713551.t: Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *pʰorā́, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoréh₂. By surface analysis, φέρω (phérō, “to bring, bear, carry”) + -η (-ē)

713573.t: Uncertain. Seems to go back to a stem *φραδ-.

713593.t: From προ- (pro-, “forwards”) + ὁράω (horáō, “to see”) + -α (-ā, action noun suffix), with shift of aspiration from the initial of ὁράω (horáō) to the initial of προ- (pro-); compare φρουρός (phrourós, “watchman”).

713549.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kʷʰónos (“murder”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰónos (“killing, slaughter”). Equal to θείνω (theínō, “to strike”) + -ος (-os).

713519.t: Of unclear origin. Traditionally linked to a large group of words beginning with φλ- (phl-), like φλέω (phléō, “to overflow, abound”), φλύω (phlúō, “to be full of juice, thrive”), and φλύκταινα (phlúktaina, “blister”).

713588.t: From φρονέω (phronéō, “to think”) + -σις (-sis); the former from φρήν (phrḗn, “mind”).

713523.t: Formally, it belongs to φλέω (phléō, “to abound”) together with φλόος (phlóos, “skin, slough”). Semantically, the connection with φλέω (phléō) is clear in ὑπέρφλοιος (hupérphloios, “luxuriant, succulent”).

713561.t: By surface analysis, φέρω (phérō, “to bring, carry”) + -ος (-os). Given the comparison with Sanskrit भर॑ (bhára), the term may be derived from Proto-Hellenic *pʰóros, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰóros (“load, burden”).

713507.t: From φιλέω (phĭléō, “to love; to kiss”) + -τρον (-tron, instrument noun suffix).

713575.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pʰrakʷjō, of unclear origin, with analysis complicated by the coexistence and apparent confluence of φρακ- (phrak-) and φαρκ- (phark-) in the verb's derivatives.

713586.t: From o-grade of the root of φρήν (phrḗn, “mind”) + -έω (-éō).

713576.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pʰrḗwər, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₁wr̥ (“well, source”) (whence Sanskrit भु॒र्वन् (bhurván, “restless movement of water”), Old Armenian աղբիւր (ałbiwr, “fountain, source”), Proto-Germanic *brunnô), from *bʰrewh₁-, which is…

713544.t: From φόνος (phónos), the o-grade of θείνω (theínō, “kill”), + -εύς (-eús, masculine agentive suffix).

713590.t: From φροντίς (phrontís, “thought”) + *-ϳω (*-jō), superficially containing -ίζω (-ízō). Related to φρήν (phrḗn).

713554.t: From φέρω (phérō, “to bear, carry; to bring, fetch”) + -έω (-éō, frequentative verbal suffix); from Proto-Hellenic *pʰoréyō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoréyeti. Cognate with Sanskrit भारयति (bhāráyati).

713584.t: According to Beekes, from the same Pre-Greek root of φρίξ (phríx, “shivering”).

713525.t: Perhaps a back-formation from φλυαρέω (phlŭāréō, “to talk nonsense”).

713508.t: Unexplained. According to Beekes, the similarity of the suffix with κημός (kēmós, “muzzle”) is notable, while the relation with φιτρός (phitrós, “block of wood”) seems improbable.

713520.t: A technical word without etymology, so possibly Pre-Greek.

713526.t: From the Pre-Greek root *φλυκτ- (*phlŭkt-) + -ις (-ĭs). Compare φλύκταινα (phlŭ́ktaină, “blister”).

713509.t: From φιμός (phīmós, “any instrument for keeping the mouth closed”) + -όω (-óō, verbal suffix).

713581.t: From the verb φρίσσω (phríssō, “to shiver, shudder, tremble”).

713562.t: From φόρτος (phórtos, “load, charge”) + -ίζω (-ĭ́zō, denominative verb suffix).
